TERMS, CONDITIONS, AND STIPULATIONS
IDAHO POWER COMPANY
SHORT-TERM RIGHT-OF-WAY
IDI-39567

Master Agreement

1. This grant is subject to the terms set forth in the Master Agreement between the U.S. Department
of the Interior, Bureau of Land Management – Idaho and Idaho Power Company for Managing
Rights-of-Way (BLM-MA-ID-001), or subsequent revisions.

General Terms

2. The Holder will indemnify the United States against any liability for damage to life or property
arising from the occupancy or use of public lands under this grant.

3. The Holder will comply with all Federal, State, tribal and/or local laws, regulations and policy
applicable to the right-of-way area.

4. The Authorized Officer may suspend or terminate in whole, or in part, any rights granted when, in
his/her judgment, conditions arise which result in the approved terms and conditions being
inadequate to protect the public health and safety or to protect the environment.

5. There is reserved to the Secretary of the Interior, or his/her lawful delegate, the right to grant
additional rights-of-way or permits for compatible uses on, over, under or adjacent to the land
involved in this grant.

6. The Holder will not interfere with public land management practices of the BLM or any authorized
BLM operators, licensees, agents or public.

7. The Holder will permit free and unrestricted public access upon the right-of-way for all lawful
purposes except for those specific areas designated as restricted by the Authorized Officer to
protect the public, wildlife, livestock, or facilities constructed within the right-of-way. No gates,
signs, barriers, obstructions, or other impediments are allowed on public lands wither within or
outside the right-of-way, unless specifically authorized or required.

8. The right-of-way will be maintained in a sanitary condition at all times; waste materials will be
disposed of promptly at an appropriate waste disposal site. 'Waste' is defined as all discarded
matter including, but not limited to, human waste, trash, garbage, refuse, oil drums, petroleum
products, ash, and equipment that are a result of the Holder's activities.

Protection of Cultural Resources

9. Pursuant to 43 CFR 10, the Holder of this authorization must immediately notify the Authorized
Officer, by telephone, with written confirmation, immediately upon the discovery of human
remains, funerary items, sacred objects, or objects of cultural patrimony. Further, pursuant to 43

CFR 10.4 (c) and (d), the Holder must stop activities in the vicinity of the discovery and protect it
until notified to proceed by the Authorized Officer. The BLM Authorized Officer will determine
avoidance, protection or mitigation measures in consultation with the Holder, Idaho SHPO, and
affected Tribes. Costs associated with the discovery, evaluation, protection or mitigation of the
discovery will be the responsibility of the Holder.

10. Any cultural and/or paleontological resource (historic or prehistoric site or object, or fossil)
discovered by the Holder, or any persons working on his behalf on public or Federal land will be
immediately reported to the Authorized Officer. Holder will suspend all operations in the immediate
area of such discovery until written authorization to proceed is issued by the Authorized Officer. An
evaluation of the discovery will be made by the Authorized Officer to determine appropriate actions
to prevent the loss of significant cultural or scientific values. The Holder will be responsible for the
cost of evaluation and mitigation, and any decision as to proper avoidance, protection, or mitigation
measures will be made by the Authorized Officer after consulting with the Holder and others under
Section 106 of the National Historic Preservation Act.

Protection of Survey Monuments

11. The Holder will protect all survey monuments found within the right-of-way. Survey monuments
include, but are not limited to, General Land Office and Bureau of Land Management Cadastral
Survey Corners, reference corners, witness points, U.S. Coastal and Geodetic benchmarks and
triangulation stations, military control monuments, and recognizable civil (both public and private)
survey monuments. In the event of obliteration or disturbance of any of the above, the Holder will
immediately report the incident, in writing, to the Authorized Officer and the respective installing
authority if known. Where General Land Office or Bureau of Land Management survey monuments
or references are obliterated during Holder's operations, the Holder will secure the services of a
registered land surveyor or Bureau cadastral surveyor to restore the disturbed monument and
references using surveying procedures found in the Manual of Surveying Instructions for the Survey
of the Public Lands of the United States, latest edition. The Holder will record such survey in the
appropriate county and send a copy to the Authorized Officer. If the Bureau cadastral surveyors or
other Federal surveyors are used to restore the disturbed survey monument, the Holder will be
responsible for the survey cost.

Hazardous Materials and Toxic Substances

12. Holder will comply with the applicable Federal and State Laws and regulations concerning the use of
pesticides (i.e. insecticides, herbicides, fungicides, rodenticide, and other similar substances) in all
activities/operations under this grant. Pesticides will be used only in accordance with their
registered uses and within the limitations imposed by the Secretary of the Interior. Prior to the use
of pesticides, the Holder will obtain from the Authorized Officer written approval of a plan showing
the type and quantity of material to be used, pest(s) to be controlled, method of application,
location of storage and disposal containers, and any other information deemed necessary by the
Authorized Officer. Pesticides will not be permanently stored on public lands authorized for use
under this grant. Applicator(s) will hold a current applicator's license or be under the direct
supervision of a licensed applicator.

13. The Holder will comply with all applicable Federal, State and local laws and regulations, existing or
hereafter enacted or promulgated, with regard to any Hazardous Material, as defined in this
paragraph, that will be used, produced, transported or stored on or within the right-of-way or any of
the right-of-way facilities, or used in the construction, operation, maintenance or termination of the
right-of-way or any of its facilities. "Hazardous material" means any substance, pollutant or
contaminant that is listed as hazardous under the Comprehensive Environmental Response,

Compensation, and Liability Act of 1980, 42 U.S.C. § 9601 et seq., as amended, (hereinafter
"CERCLA") and its regulations. The definition of hazardous substances under CERCLA includes any
"hazardous waste" as defined in the Resource Conservation and Recovery Act of 1976, 42 U.S.C. §
6901 et seq., as amended, (hereinafter “RCRA”) and its regulations. The term hazardous material
also includes any nuclear or byproduct material as defined by the Atomic Energy Act of 1954, 42 U.
S. C. § 2011 et seq., as amended. The term does not include petroleum, including crude oil or any
fraction thereof that is not otherwise specifically listed or designated as a hazardous substance
under CERCLA section 101(14), 42 U.S.C. § 9601(14), nor does the term include natural gas.

14. The Holder agrees to indemnify the United States against any liability arising from the release of any
hazardous substance or hazardous waste (as these terms are defined in the Comprehensive
Environmental Response, Compensation and Liability Act of 1980, 42 U.S.C. § 9601, et seq. or the
Resource Conservation and Recovery Act of 1976, 42 U.S.C. § 6901 et seq.) on the right-of-way
(unless the release or threatened release is wholly unrelated to the right-of-way Holder's activity on
the right-of-way). This agreement applies without regard to whether a release is caused by the
Holder, its agent, or unrelated third parties.

15. The Holder(s) will comply with the Toxic Substances Control Act of 1976 as amended, 15 U.S.C. §
2601 et seq. (1982) with regards to any toxic substances that are used, generated by or stored on
the right-of-way or on facilities authorized under this right-of-way grant. (See 40 CFR Part 702-799
and especially, provisions on polychlorinated biphenyls, 40 CFR 761.1-761.193.) Additionally, any
release of toxic substances (leaks, spills, etc.) in excess of the reportable quantity established by 40
CFR Part 117 will be reported as required by the Comprehensive Environmental Response,
Compensation, and Liability Act, section 102b. A copy of any report required or requested by any
Federal agency or State government as a result of a reportable release or spill of any toxic
substances will be furnished to the Authorized Officer concurrent with the filing of the reports to the
involved Federal agency or State government.

Fire Prevention and Control

16. When performing construction and maintenance (including emergency repairs) activities during the
"closed" fire season (May 10 – October 20), as set by Idaho State Law, Title 38-115, or during any
other closed fire season prescribed by the BLM Idaho State Director, the Holder, including those
working on their behalf, will equip at least one on-site vehicle with firefighting equipment, including,
but not limited to, fire suppression hand tools (i.e. shovels, rakes, Pulaski's, etc.), a 16-20 pound fire
extinguisher, and a sufficient supply of water for initial attack, with a mechanism to effectively spray
the water (i.e. backpack pumps, watersprayer, etc.)

17. Within the bound of the right-of-way, the Holder will provide and maintain a vegetation clearance of
up to 20 feet around the base of wood poles or other facilities with the potential to catch and/or
spread fire.

18. During conditions of extreme fire danger or when the State of Idaho and/or the BLM Idaho State
Director issues a fire restriction order, operations will be limited or suspended in specific areas, or
additional measures may be required by the Authorized Officer.

19. In accordance with 43 CFR 2805.12(d) (or subsequent revisions), the Holder will do everything
reasonable to prevent wildfires on or in the immediate vicinity of the right-of-way. The Holder will
immediately report fires to the BLM Authorized Officer or Fire Dispatch (800-974-2373), and take all

necessary fire suppression actions, when safe to do so, with their personnel and equipment on any
fires they cause to ignite.

20. During or following initial attack, the Holder will report to the Fire Investigator or BLM Incident
Commander and will not enter into the origin area on BLM fires unless given permission to do so.

21. The Holder will collaborate and cooperate with the BLM in its efforts to investigate, suppress and
respond to all future wildland fires. The duty to "collaborate” and “cooperate" includes, but is not
limited to, the following duties regardless of whether BLM is on the scene:
a. The duty to provide the BLM (Authorized Officer or local fire dispatch center) with
reasonable and timely notice concerning all wildland fires involving the Holder's facilities, or
discovered during routine operations.
b. The duty to share factual information with the BLM concerning the wildland fires, including
but not limited to the names of Holder's employees with knowledge of the incident; and to
allow employees to be interviewed by BLM's investigators regarding factual information
relating to a wildland fire.
c. The duty to reasonably account for Holder's actions taken at the scene of a wildland fire.
d. The duty to minimize disturbance of potential evidence located on the scene; to properly
handle and preserve any evidence collected; to not engage in any destructive testing
without BLM's consent; and to make all evidence available to the BLM in a rapid and timely
manner.
e. The duty to not hamper the BLM investigation of origin and cause of the wildland fire; and
to reasonably assist BLM's investigation at the scene.
f. The duty to provide information concerning the construction, maintenance and/or repairs of
any Holder's facilities located at or adjacent to a wildland fire.
g. The duty during BLM fire suppression efforts: to defer to and follow the instructions of the
BLM's Incident Commander regarding activities within the boundaries of the wildland fire
and checking in and out of the wildland fire; and to recognize BLM;s primary authority over
the scene.

Operations and Maintenance

22. The Holder will conduct all activities associated with the operation, maintenance, and termination of
the right-of-way within the authorized limits of the right-of-way. If at any time the Holder wishes to
reconstruct or relocate any portion of the right-of-way, or the improvements thereon, in a manner
that has been determined to be a substantial deviation, prior written authorization must be
obtained from the Authorized Officer.

23. Specific sites as identified by the Authorized Officer (e.g., archaeological sites, areas with threatened
and endangered species, or fragile watersheds) where construction equipment and vehicles are not
allowed will be clearly marked onsite by the Holder before any surface disturbing activities begin.
The Holder will be responsible for assuring that construction personnel are well trained to recognize
these markers and understand the equipment movement restrictions involved.

24. No surface disturbing maintenance activities will be allowed within riparian conservation area
buffers, as follows: 300 feet for fish-bearing streams; 150 feet for perennial non-fish bearing
streams; 150 feet for ponds, lakes, reservoirs, and wetlands greater than 1 acre; 50 feet for
seasonally-flowing or intermittent streams, wetlands less than 1 acre, or landslide-prone areas. Any
deviation from this requirement will have the prior written approval of the Authorized Officer.

25. The Holder will remove only the minimum amount of vegetation and/or topsoil necessary for the
construction and/or maintenance of structures and facilities. Topsoil removed will be stockpiled
within the right-of-way or at an approved location during excavation and reused as cover on
disturbed areas to facilitate growth of vegetation.

26. Construction holes left open overnight will be covered. Covers will be secured in place and will be
strong enough to prevent livestock or wildlife from falling through and into a hole.

27. If any emergency repair activity results in disturbance outside the right-of-way boundary, the Holder
will notify the Authorized Officer within three days of the occurrence. Upon review, the Authorized
Officer may require remediation.

28. The Holder will notify the Authorized Officer at least 90 days prior to any non-emergency activities
that would cause surface disturbance in the right-of-way. Surface disturbing activities are not
considered routine maintenance. The Authorized Officer will determine if resource inventories,
treatments, or mitigation are required for the activity. The Holder will be responsible for the cost of
inventory, avoidance, treatment or mitigation, including and maintenance-cause damage. The
Authorized Officer will determine avoidance, treatment and mitigation measures that are necessary
after consulting with the Holder.

Access

29. New access roads or cross-country vehicle travel outside the right-of-way will not be permitted
without prior written approval by the Authorized Officer. The Holder will obtain a right-of-way to
use any roads outside the right-of-way that require surface-disturbing repair or maintenance.

Avian Protection

30. Operations and maintenance within the right-of-way will comply with the most current nest
management guidelines provided by the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (USFWS) as clarified in ID-IB-
2010-039, or most recent guidance. If proposed maintenance activities are located within one mile
of bald or golden eagle nests, the Holder will coordinate with the BLM and the USFWS to determine
the likelihood of disturbance and any appropriate measures necessary to comply with the Band and
Golden Eagle Protection Act (16 U.S.C. § et seq.).

31. To the extent possible, operations and maintenance activities that include ground disturbance
and/or vegetation removal will be conducted either prior to or following the affected migratory bird
nesting season (January 1 - July 31 along the canyon rim) to avoid and/or minimize take of
migratory birds as defined in the Migratory Bird Treaty Act (MBTA) of 1918 (16 U.S.C. § 703 et seq.)
as amended. If any ground disturbing activities must occur during the nesting season (e.g., soil
disturbance or vegetation removal), the Holder will coordinate with the BLM and USFWS to
determine appropriate measures to comply with the MBTA.

32. Unless otherwise agreed to by the Authorized Officer in writing, power lines will be constructed or
rebuilt in accordance with the most recent version of the report, Suggested Practices for Avian
Protection on Power Lines (Avian Power Line Interaction Committee, 2006). The Holder will assume
the burden and expense of proving that pole designs not shown in the above publication are "eagle
safe." Such proof will be provided by a qualified raptor biologist approved by the Authorized Officer.
The BLM reserved the right to require modifications or additions to all power line structures placed
within this right-of-way, should they be necessary to ensure the safety of large perching birds. Such

modifications and/or additions will be made by the Holder without liability or expense to the United
States.

Plants

33. The Holder will be responsible for the control of noxious weeds and non-native invasive plants that
result from construction, use, or maintenance authorized in the Holder's right-of-way grant. The
Holder must coordinate with the Authorized Officer and/or local authorities for acceptable weed
control measures (within limits imposed in the grant stipulations) prior to implementing weed
treatments.

34. The Holder will use only BLM-approved herbicide and adjuvants, and the applicator(s) will hold a
current State of Idaho applicator's license or be under the direct supervision of a licensed applicator.

35. The Holder will clean equipment, machinery and vehicles that disturb soil or vegetation prior to
entry into BLM-managed lands. Cleaning is defined as removal of all dirt, grease, plant parts and
material that may carry seeds or plant material from tires, tracks, belly plates, undercarriages, etc.
Pressure washing is recommended. To the extent practical, the Holder will avoid or minimize travel
through or parking in areas infested with noxious weeds to avoid spreading seeds or plant parts. At
the BLM's discretion, equipment, machinery, and vehicles may be inspected prior to entry onto
BLM-managed lands.

36. The Holder will seed all disturbed areas with a seed mixture(s) and application method approved by
the Authorized Officer to enhance successful germination and seedling establishment to control
invasive species. The seed mixture(s) will be applied in the amounts specified in pounds of pure live
seed (PLS)/acre. Seed will be tested and the viability of testing seed will be done within State law(s)
and within 6 months prior to purchase. Commercial seed will be certified “weed free". The seed
mixture contain will be tagged in accordance with State law(s) and available for inspection by the
Authorized Officer.

37. The Holder may clear brush and remove hazard trees less than 8 inches in Diameter Breast Height
(DBH) within the ROW if necessary for operation and maintenance and/or for the health and safety
of the Holder and his/her agents. Trees 8 inch DBH or greater within the ROW, and potential hazard
trees outside the ROW, will be marked by the Holder. Prior to harvest, hazard trees outside the
ROW and trees 8 inch DBH or greater will be verified and measured by the Authorized Officer.
Vegetation and timber that is cut remains the property of the Government (43 CFR 2805.15) and
may be sold to the Holder for appraised value in accordance with 43 CFR 5400.

Pursuant to Section 512(e) of the Federal Land Policy and Management Act of 1976 (Public Law 115-
141), if vegetation or hazard trees have contacted or present an imminent danger of contacting an
electric transmission or distribution line from within or adjacent to the ROW, the Holder may prune
or remove the vegetation or hazard tree to avoid the disruption of electric service and eliminate
immediate fire and safety hazards. In this case, the Holder will notify the local BLM field or district
office no later than 1 day after the date of the response to emergency conditions.

Termination and Final Rehabilitation

38. When the right-of-way is no longer required for the purpose granted, the Holder will submit a
termination and rehabilitation plan to the Authorized Officer. This plan will include, but is not
limited to, removal of facilities, structures, and surface material, re-contouring, topsoiling, and/or
seeding. The Authorized Officer must approve the plan in writing prior to commencement of any

termination activities, and may request a joint inspection of the right-of-way prior to
development/acceptance of such a plan, and/or following execution of such a plan.

RECORD OF CATEGORICAL EXCLUSION DETERMINATION

A. Proposed Action: Western proposes to conduct pole replacement along the
existing Electrical District #2-Saguaro #1 115-kV transmission line. This will consist
of removing ninety-five (95) deteriorated wood poles by lifting or pulling them from
the ground, auger a 24" hole and installing new wood pole structures and associated
hardware. Western will use dozers, backhoes, front end loaders, dump trucks, trailer
trucks, water trucks, bucket trucks, crew trucks and pickup trucks to bring crews and
equipment to the project area. This work is necessary to maintain the safety and
reliability of the bulk electrical system.

The attached maps show the project areas are situated within Sections 30 & 31
Township 6 South Range 8 East, Sections 6, 7, 18, 19, 30 & 31 Township 7 South
Range 8 East, Sections 6, 7, 18, 19, 30 & 31 Township 8 South Range 8 East,
Sections 6, 7, 18, 19, 30, 31, 32, 33, 34, 35 & 36 Township 9 South Range 8 East,
Sections 30, 31, 32 & 33 Township 9 South Range 9 East, Sections 3, 4, 10, 11 &
12 Township 10 South Range 9 East, Sections 7, 15, 16 & 17 Township 10 South
Range 10 East on the Gila and Salt River Meridian, Pinal County, Arizona. Work will
be conducted within Western's right of way. The corresponding U.S.G.S. 7.5-minute
topographic maps are Eloy North, Eloy South, Friendly Corners, Samaniego Hills &
Red Rock, Arizona. This work is planned to begin the month of November, 2011.

B. Categorical Exclusion Applied: 10 CFR, Part 1021, Subpart D, Appendix B, B1.3:
"Routine maintenance activities and custodial services for buildings, structures,
rights-of-way, infrastructures (e.g., pathways, roads, and railroads), vehicles and
equipment, and localized vegetation and pest control, during which operations may
be suspended and resumed. Custodial services are activities to preserve facility
appearance, working conditions, and sanitation, such as cleaning, window washing,
lawn mowing, trash collection, painting, and snow removal. Routine maintenance
activities, corrective (that is, repair), preventive, and predictive, are required to
maintain and preserve buildings, structures, infrastructures, and equipment
in a condition suitable for a facility to be used for its designated purpose. Routine
maintenance may result in replacement to the extent that replacement is in kind and
is not a substantial upgrade or improvement. In kind replacement includes
installation of new components to replace outmoded components if the replacement
does not result in a significant change in the expected useful life, design capacity, or
function of the facility. Routine maintenance does not include replacement of a major
component that significantly extends the originally intended useful life of a facility

It is my decision to implement the Proposed Action, as described in DOI-BLM-CO-N010-2021-

near the Little Snake/White River Field Office boundary. The repair is expected to consist of
layering compatible rock material and BLM-approved Geotech material, then installing a culvert
and armoring the inlet and outlet of the culvert with local rock material from a nearby rock pile,
within BLM standards. The road repairs are expected to be completed by a contractor using
standard road maintenance equipment (e.g., excavators, dozers, wheel loaders, and motor
graders), and is expected to be completed by August 2021.

disturbance will be no more than three feet below grade. On-site material will be used where
possible, including native rock from a rock pile approximately one mile northeast of the failure
site (CX Appendix A, Figure 1). Construction activities will occur within 50 feet of the existing
road. Some road closures during construction are unavoidable but the BLM will communicate
these closures to the public in advance.

Cultural Resources: The National Historic Preservation Act requires that federal land managing
agencies consider the effect of federal undertakings on historic and prehistoric sites that are
eligible to the National Register of Historic Places (NHRP). A review of existing records was
completed to determine the extent of previous cultural resource surveys and the location of
recorded sites in relation to the road repair and native rock pile locations. A small number (three:
MC.E.R12/21-85; MC.LM.R45/13-81; MF.LM.R249/10-94) of previous cultural inventories
occurred within a one-mile radius around the two locations; none of which intersected with the
proposed project areas. While cultural inventories in the area are limited, they did reveal
moderate site density around Sagebrush Draw; therefore, a Class III pedestrian survey was
warranted.
On May 8, 2021, BLM Colorado Northwest District archaeologist Wendy Parker surveyed a
total of 1.6 acres (0.8 acres at each location) around the road damage and rock pile locations. The
survey yielded negative results; therefore, the undertaking would have no effect on historic
properties and no further archaeological work is necessary.
Native American Religious Concerns: Lacking a written, formal agreement outlining a
consultation process between BLM-LSFO and the relevant tribes, the field office policy is to
consult with tribes when the proposed undertaking is within or in the vicinity of an area known
to be of concern to the tribes or when the undertaking involves sites of the kind that experience
has shown would be of tribal concern. Such sites include burials, rock art, wickiups, stone circle
sites, possible vision quest sites, possible eagle traps, etc. As the road damage and rock
procurement area is not in or near an area of known concern to the tribes, nor would it be in the
vicinity of sites of the kind that are of tribal concern, it is concluded that proposed undertaking
would not affect areas or sites of Native American concern.

title: National Environmental Policy Act
text:
As the U.S. expands clean energy and modernizes its infrastructure, the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) plays a critical role. Recently, it has become a focal point in policy debates—often misunderstood, mischaracterized, and used as a proxy for larger political battles. While CATF has identified opportunities for efficiency and improvement in the environmental review process, NEPA can support rapid, responsible clean energy deployment while centering communities and the environment.


NEPA is a foundational environmental law that has, for more than fifty years, ensured that federal agencies consider the environmental impacts of a proposed major federal action. NEPA does not mandate particular outcomes or standards; instead, it requires federal agencies to consider the reasonably foreseeable environmental impacts of their activities, integrate those considerations into agency decision making, and enhance public transparency in the decision-making process. ​NEPA reviews are also often integrated with implementation of other bedrock statutes, such as the Endangered Species Act, Clean Air Act, Clean Water Act, and National Historic Preservation Act. ​



The NEPA process is a mandatory decision-making process that requires federal agencies to consider the potential impacts of proposed “major federal actions” before committing resources. Major federal actions are those subject to an agency’s control and responsibility; for clean energy infrastructure projects, when NEPA is triggered, it is often because a project is located on or crosses federal or Tribal trust land or receives federal grants or loans.
For example, if the federal government is considering whether to grant the right-of-way for a new transmission line to cross federal land, which will connect energy projects to the grid, NEPA requires the agency to evaluate how the project might affect local ecosystems, cultural resources, nearby communities, and other resource areas, and document that analysis in an environmental review. Although limited by recent agency changes, the public should then have an opportunity to review and comment on the agency’s analysis before a final decision is made.





NEPA is often scapegoated as a core cause of infrastructure delays and cancellations. However, arguments that blame NEPA for permitting delays mischaracterize the empirical reality. Where projects are subject to NEPA, evidence shows that NEPA in fact improves environmental decision making and may actually improve overall permitting efficiency by providing a coordination mechanism among federal agencies. Indeed, most delays are the result of factors other than NEPA itself, such as lack of sufficient staffing, budget, and coordination at federal agencies; project-specific elements (e.g., supply chain constraints); and lack of alignment in state and local permitting requirements.



Most solar and onshore wind projects in the United States are not subject to NEPA. One recent study found that less than five percent of onshore wind and solar projects constructed between 2010 and 2021 required a comprehensive environment review under NEPA or a project-specific permit under the Clean Water Act or Endangered Species Act.
Because they are sited in federal waters, all offshore wind projects are subject to NEPA review. Geothermal projects are overwhelmingly located on federal land, which triggers a NEPA review, and indeed separate NEPA reviews may be required for each phase of development.
Transmission lines sometimes cross federal lands or receive federal funding, with a resulting 26 percent of all new electric transmission line miles from 2010-2020 requiring an environmental impact statement.



NEPA established the Council on Environmental Quality (CEQ), which oversees the law’s implementation across the government. Each individual federal agency, in consultation with CEQ, has the responsibility to develop its own NEPA procedures. Individual agencies are also responsible for conducting NEPA reviews.
For more than 40 years, CEQ-issued NEPA regulations promoted consistency across the federal government. In early 2025, following an executive order, CEQ rescinded those regulations. Federal agencies soon followed suit, with many rescinding their existing NEPA regulations and replacing them with agency-specific nonbinding procedural guidance. For now, the NEPA landscape is that of a patchwork of differing implementing procedures across agencies.



CATF research has identified numerous evidence-based ways to improve and streamline permitting and environmental reviews while maintaining public participation and rigorous scientific standards. These include finding new efficiencies in the NEPA process, such as transparent and rigorous consideration of regulatory categorical exclusions, tiering of reviews, and eliminating redundancies. Agencies and developers should also conduct
early, sustained, and meaningful stakeholder engagement, which helps to ensure that projects avoid unnecessary opposition and delays.
Meaningful reform to permitting and environmental review processes will not improve outcomes unless it addresses the challenges caused by leadership gaps, inconsistent and inadequate funding, a lack of sufficient staff with permitting expertise in agency headquarters and field offices, and insufficient coordination among federal agencies. Undermining NEPA will worsen environmental outcomes while bringing us no closer to clean energy deployment at scale.




Recent actions across all three branches of government have restricted the scope of NEPA implementation by creating disparate processes, limiting public engagement, and weakening the scientific robustness of reviews. These rollbacks risk:
Reducing community input in decisions that directly affect public health and environment, which erodes trust in the clean energy transition

Increasing litigation risk, which can delay projects
Heightening uncertainty for developers, which increases project timelines and costs
Tracking NEPA-related developments in the Trump administration





2025-01-20: Executive Order 14154 (“Unleashing American Energy”) revokes the 1977 order directing CEQ to issue NEPA regulations and instructs agencies to eliminate permitting delays.
2025-01-20: Executive Order 14156 (“Declaring a National Energy Emergency”) directs agencies to use emergency permitting provisions to expedite approvals for energy and infrastructure projects (excluding wind and solar).
2025-02-19: CEQ issues guidance instructing agencies to revise or establish NEPA procedures prioritizing efficiency and certainty over other policy objectives.
2025-02-25: CEQ issues an interim final rule removing its NEPA implementing regulations from the Code of Federal Regulations.
2025-04-11: CEQ interim final rule takes effect; CEQ NEPA regulations are formally removed from the CFR.
2025-04-15: Presidential memorandum directs CEQ to issue a Permitting Technology Action Plan and establish an interagency Permitting Innovation Center.
2025-04-23: Department of the Interior announces emergency permitting procedures reducing review timelines to under one month; CEQ concurs that the procedures comply with NEPA.
2025-05-01: House Committee on Natural Resources releases reconciliation draft including pay-to-play permitting provision (125% review cost in exchange for deadlines and no judicial review).
2025-05-22: House of Representatives passes reconciliation bill including pay-to-play permitting provisions.
2025-05-23: DOI uses emergency permitting for the first time, approving the Utah Velvet-Wood uranium and vanadium mine in 14 days.
2025-05-29: Supreme Court decides Seven County Infrastructure Coalition v. Eagle County, Colorado, holding that agencies may limit NEPA review to matters within their decisional authority and courts should defer to agencies on scope.
2025-05-30: CEQ releases the Permitting Technology Action Plan.
2025-06-04: Senate Committee on Environment and Public Works releases reconciliation draft retaining pay-to-play permitting and rescinding permitting funds to agencies.
2025-06-05: CEQ launches the Categorical Exclusion Explorer, a public database of agency categorical exclusions under NEPA.
2025-06-19: Senate parliamentarian rules that eliminating judicial review under pay-to-play permitting violates the Byrd Rule and would require 60 votes.
2025-07-01: Senate passes reconciliation bill (51–50) allowing pay-to-play expedited reviews subject to judicial review.
2025-07-03: House passes the Senate version of the reconciliation bill without changes.
2025-07-03: DOE, DOI, USDA, Army Corps of Engineers, DOT, and FERC introduce new NEPA implementing procedures, generally converting regulations into nonbinding guidance.
2025-07-04: President Trump signs the reconciliation bill into law.
2025-07-22: House Committee on Natural Resources holds oversight hearing titled “Permitting Purgatory: Restoring Common Sense to NEPA Reviews.”
2025-07-23: White House releases AI Action Plan and President Trump signs executive order on AI data center infrastructure directing agencies to establish new categorical exclusions and presuming NEPA exemption when federal funding is under 50%.
2025-07-25: Introduction of the SPEED Act, proposing limits on judicial review, exclusions from NEPA for certain federally funded or state-reviewed projects, and limits on late-stage scientific information.
2025-09-10: House Committee on Natural Resources holds a hearing on the SPEED Act, ePermit Act, and Studying NEPA’s Impact on Projects Act.
2025-09-29: CEQ issues updated NEPA implementation guidance and an agency procedures template, replacing February guidance.
2025-11-20: House Committee on Natural Resources marks up eight bills (including SPEED Act, ePermit Act, and Studying NEPA’s Impact on Projects Act); all pass out of committee.
2025-12-09: ePermit Act and Studying NEPA’s Impact on Projects Act pass the House by unanimous voice vote.
2025-12-10: Passed ePermit Act and Studying NEPA’s Impact on Projects Act are referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee.
2025-12-15: During House Rules Committee consideration, amendment limits permit certainty provisions from applying retroactively to actions between 2025-01-20 and enactment.
2025-12-16: American Clean Power Association withdraws support for the SPEED Act following the retroactivity amendment.
2025-12-18: SPEED Act passes the House 221–196 and is referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee.
2025-12-22: Department of the Interior issues stop-work orders for five offshore wind projects, including Vineyard Wind 1.
2025-12-22: Senators Sheldon Whitehouse and Martin Heinrich issue a statement condemning the stop-work orders and warning that permitting reform talks cannot proceed if existing permits are ignored.
2026-01-08: CEQ adopts as final its February 2025 interim rule removing NEPA regulations from the Federal Register, without changes.

title: Phase 2 Deliverable Assessment
text:
Date: 2026-02-11



Before diving into each deliverable, the overarching lessons from Phase 1 are critical:

Messy, unstructured data is the constant enemy. Metadata is sparse, text formats are inconsistent across agencies, and even “simple” extraction tasks (like finding a decision date with a signature block) required multi-iteration pipeline development (regex -> hybrid LLM -> BERT -> 11+ refinements).
Initiation-style tasks (finding implicit information) are far harder than decision-style tasks (finding explicit information). BERT decision coverage hit 85%, but initiation stalled at 16% – and that gap persists despite extensive pattern expansion and class rebalancing. Phase 2 deliverables lean heavily toward the “initiation” end of this spectrum (implicit, contextual, requires reasoning).
Local LLMs (Llama 3.2 3B) work for classification but struggle with comprehension. The hybrid timeline approach showed this clearly: the LLM can label “is this a decision date?” but it can’t reliably reason about why a project triggered NEPA or what constitutes significant impact.
Every extraction task took 2-3x the initially estimated time once you factor in validation, false positive triage, class imbalance, and re-runs.







Difficulty: MODERATE-HIGH
What it requires: For each project, identify why NEPA was triggered – federal land, federal funding, federal permits, or some combination. This means reading project documents and classifying the federal nexus.
What works in your favor: - The lead agency is already in the metadata and is often a strong proxy (BLM -> federal land; DOE -> federal funding). You could get 60-70% coverage from metadata-based heuristics alone before touching document text. - The “trigger” language is sometimes explicit: “This EA is prepared because the proposed action involves a federal lease on BLM-managed land.” - Regex can catch many explicit patterns.
Problems I foresee: - Many documents don’t explicitly state why NEPA was triggered – the federal nexus is assumed by context. A CE for a cell tower on National Forest land doesn’t say “because it’s on federal land”; it just says “Coldfoot Cell Tower, Tongass National Forest.” - Distinguishing “mentioned” from “triggered by” is hard. A project might discuss federal funding in one section but the actual trigger is federal land use. - Multiple triggers per project is common and ambiguous. - 445K targeted pages is large. Even with 30% prefiltering, you’re sending ~134K pages to an LLM. - A local 3B model likely can’t do this well. This is a comprehension/inference task, not just pattern matching.
Realistic time estimate: 35-50 hours
High-level plan:

Build a metadata-based heuristic classifier (agency -> trigger type mapping) – covers the easy cases (~60-70%) (5 hrs)
Develop regex patterns for explicit trigger language (“federal land,” “DOE funding,” “Section 404 permit,” etc.) (5 hrs)
Run regex extraction on the full corpus with prefiltering (3 hrs)
For ambiguous/missing cases, design an LLM prompt and test on a 50-project sample – evaluate whether Llama 3B is sufficient or you need an enterprise model (8 hrs)
Full LLM run on remaining unresolved cases (5 hrs)
Manual validation on a stratified sample of ~50-100 projects (5 hrs)
Iterate on false positives/negatives, re-run (5-10 hrs)
Analysis & visualization (4 hrs)





Difficulty: HIGH – This is the hardest deliverable and the highest risk
What it requires: For FEIS/DEIS documents, extract which resource areas (air quality, water, wildlife, cultural resources, etc.) were found to have “significant impacts.” Then, starting with mitigated FONSIs, identify cases where impacts would have been significant but were mitigated.
What works in your favor: - EIS documents are relatively structured – they typically have chapters organized by resource area (Chapter 3: Affected Environment, Chapter 4: Environmental Consequences). - The vocabulary of significance is somewhat formulaic (“significant adverse impact,” “less than significant with mitigation,” etc.). - Only ~371K pages from FEIS/DEIS documents, which is a smaller subset.
Problems I foresee – and they are serious: - No standard format across agencies. DOI, DOE, USDA, DOD all structure their impact analyses differently. Some use tables, some use narrative, some use a hybrid. Section numbering varies. - Significance language is highly nuanced. “The proposed action would result in significant impacts to…” vs. “The proposed action would not result in significant impacts to…” – these differ by one word. Worse, many documents use hedging: “potentially significant,” “significant but mitigable,” “significant and unavoidable.” - Mitigated FONSIs are exceptionally tricky. You need to identify that (a) an EA found potentially significant impacts, AND (b) mitigation measures reduced them below significance, AND (c) the FONSI was issued with conditions. This is a multi-step reasoning chain. - A 3B local model will almost certainly fail at this task. This requires reading comprehension, not pattern matching. The distinction between “significant” and “not significant” in environmental documents is exactly the kind of nuanced language understanding that requires a large model. - Resource area segmentation adds another dimension – you’re not just classifying significance for the whole document, but for ~10-15 different resource areas per document.
Realistic time estimate: 55-75 hours
This is where I’d most strongly recommend budgeting for enterprise LLMs (GPT-4o, Claude Sonnet). The $115 estimate in the proposal assumes cost-efficient mini models with 30% prefiltering – but the accuracy of a mini model on this task will likely be poor, and you may need the full-capability model. At GPT-4o pricing, 371K pages could run $300-500+ depending on context length.
High-level plan:

Define the taxonomy of resource areas and significance levels (with client input) (3 hrs)
Identify the structural patterns of EIS chapters across the top 5-6 agencies – map how they organize resource area analysis (6 hrs)
Build a document structure parser that identifies relevant sections/chapters (avoiding appendices, references, etc.) (8 hrs)
Design the LLM extraction prompt – test on 20 FEIS documents with both a local model and an enterprise model, compare accuracy (8 hrs)
Decision point: If local model accuracy is <70%, switch to enterprise LLM (likely outcome)
Full extraction run with enterprise LLM, focusing on identified relevant sections (6 hrs)
Mitigated FONSI sub-pipeline: identify FONSIs with mitigation conditions, extract the resource areas and mitigation types (10 hrs additional – this is essentially a second extraction task)
Validation on a stratified sample (5 hrs)
Analysis & visualization (5 hrs)





Difficulty: MODERATE
What it requires: Compare fossil fuel vs. clean energy and linear vs. non-linear project reviews across CE/EA/EIS rates, timelines, geography, and other dimensions.
What works in your favor: - This is primarily an analytical/comparative deliverable, not an extraction one. Most of the underlying data already exists from Phase 1. - The energy type classification is already built (clean/fossil/other). - Linear vs. non-linear can be derived from existing project type tags (transmission, pipelines = linear; generation = non-linear). - The 788K page count in the proposal seems high – this may be for validation or supplementary extraction, but the core analysis uses already-extracted data.
Problems I foresee: - Depends heavily on timeline quality. If initiation coverage remains at 16%, the timeline comparisons between fossil fuel and clean energy will be based on incomplete data. Duration statistics could be misleading. - Sample sizes for some categories may be small. Fossil fuel EIS projects vs. clean energy EIS projects – are there enough of each for meaningful comparison? - The “visual impacts” mention in the proposal is vague and could turn into a significant extraction task if it means actually identifying visual impact discussions in documents.
Realistic time estimate: 30-40 hours
High-level plan:

Create the linear/non-linear classification from existing project types (3 hrs)
Merge all Phase 1 + Phase 2 extracted datasets (timelines, capacity, reviews, geography) (4 hrs)
Build comparison tables: CE/EA/EIS rates by fossil vs. clean, linear vs. non-linear (5 hrs)
Timeline comparison analysis (duration by energy type, project type) – depends on D4 timeline quality (6 hrs)
Geographic analysis: where do fossil vs. clean energy reviews happen? (4 hrs)
Statistical testing and visualization (6 hrs)
Write-up and narrative (5 hrs)





Difficulty: MODERATE-HIGH
What it requires: Extend the Phase 1 BERT timeline pipeline to categorical exclusions (CEs), cross-reference Federal Register NOIs, and perform segmentation/outlier analysis.
What works in your favor: - The BERT pipeline infrastructure is built and battle-tested. - Decision coverage is decent at 85%. - Federal Register linking code already exists (code/extract/federal_register.py, data/analysis/noi_federal_register.parquet). - The segmentation analysis (pre/post-FRA, by agency, by year) is straightforward once timelines exist.
Problems I foresee: - CE documents are fundamentally different from EA/EIS documents. They’re often 1-3 page forms, sometimes with checkbox dates, sometimes with no narrative at all. The current regex/BERT approach was tuned for EA/EIS-style documents with signature blocks and narrative text. CE forms may need a different extraction approach entirely. - Initiation remains the Achilles’ heel. At 16% coverage, you can’t compute meaningful durations for most projects. The Phase 1 experience suggests this won’t improve dramatically without manual labeling or fundamentally different data sources (like Federal Register NOIs). - Federal Register NOI matching is fuzzy. Matching a NEPATEC project to its corresponding Federal Register NOI requires name/agency/date matching, which is error-prone. - CE projects are the vast majority (~20K of ~22K clean energy projects) but many may have trivially short timelines, skewing any aggregate analysis.
Realistic time estimate: 30-45 hours
High-level plan:

Analyze a sample of 50 CE documents to understand their structure and date patterns – determine if BERT approach transfers or needs adaptation (5 hrs)
If CE forms need new patterns: expand regex patterns, regenerate training data, retrain BERT (8 hrs)
Run BERT on full CE corpus (1-2 hrs compute time)
Federal Register NOI cross-referencing: improve fuzzy matching, validate on sample (6 hrs)
Use NOI dates as initiation fallback where BERT initiation is missing (3 hrs)
Segmentation analysis: pre/post-FRA, by agency, by project type, by year (5 hrs)
Outlier identification and case study selection (4 hrs)
Visualization (3 hrs)





Difficulty: MODERATE (but open-ended)
What it requires: Cluster FONSI documents by project type and mitigation measures to identify patterns that could support new categorical exclusion (CE) development.
What works in your favor: - Only 5,760 pages – orders of magnitude smaller than other deliverables. - FONSIs are relatively short, structured documents. - Modern embedding models (even local ones) can produce good document representations for clustering. - The client has a clear use case (supporting regulatory CE development), which gives the analysis a target.
Problems I foresee: - “Patterns” is vague. What constitutes a useful pattern for CE development? This needs careful scoping with the client. Are you looking for: project types that routinely get FONSIs (suggesting they could be CEs)? Common mitigation conditions? Resource areas that consistently come up? - Mitigation measure extraction is itself an NLP task. Mitigation conditions vary from “The project shall install erosion control barriers” to “The applicant agrees to the following 47 conditions…” – extracting and categorizing these could be a full pipeline. - Clustering can produce garbage. If the document features aren’t well-chosen, you’ll get clusters that don’t mean anything actionable.
Realistic time estimate: 18-30 hours (depends on how deep the client wants to go)
High-level plan:

Scope with client: define what “patterns” means for CE development – what would an actionable finding look like? (2 hrs)
Extract FONSI document text, filter to main document body (3 hrs)
Generate document embeddings (can start with local sentence-transformers model) (2 hrs)
Cluster analysis: try topic modeling (LDA) and embedding-based clustering (k-means on embeddings) (4 hrs)
Identify cluster themes and validate with domain knowledge (3 hrs)
If mitigation extraction is in scope: regex + LLM pipeline for mitigation conditions (6 hrs)
Synthesize findings into actionable recommendations (3 hrs)





Difficulty: MODERATE (time-consuming but well-scoped)

Deliverable 2 (Significant Impact) is the highest risk. It’s fundamentally a reading comprehension task on messy, agency-specific document formats. This is the one most likely to require an enterprise LLM, exceed its hour budget, AND still produce accuracy below expectations. I would flag this to the client as requiring a scoping conversation about acceptable accuracy levels.
The $750 LLM budget is probably too low. If Deliverable 2 requires GPT-4o-class models rather than mini models, and if prefiltering is less effective than assumed (messy text -> noisier filtering), the real LLM cost could be $1,000-2,000. The $500-1,000 range mentioned in the proposal is more realistic as a floor.
Timeline initiation remains a structural bottleneck. Deliverables 3 and 4 both depend on having good duration data, which requires good initiation dates. At 16% coverage, duration statistics are based on a small, potentially biased subset. The Federal Register NOI cross-referencing is the most promising path to improving this, but fuzzy matching introduces its own error rate.
The 180-200 hour estimate could easily become 250-300. Phase 1 taught that extraction from unstructured NEPA documents takes 2-3x longer than expected. The proposal’s internal breakdown sums to 190 hours, which assumes first-pass success on most deliverables. Budget a 30-50% overrun buffer.
Scope creep from “case study” and “outlier investigation” tasks. The timeline deliverable mentions investigating outliers through case studies – this is open-ended work that can expand indefinitely. Scope it tightly.





The concern about needing enterprise-level LLMs is well-founded, particularly for Deliverable 2. The Phase 1 experience with local Llama 3.2 3B showed that it works for classification (decision/initiation/other) but struggles with nuanced comprehension. Deliverable 2 (significance determinations) and to a lesser extent Deliverable 1 (NEPA triggers in ambiguous cases) are comprehension tasks, not classification tasks. The good news is that the rest of the infrastructure – regex prefiltering, BERT for scale, Quarto reporting, the combined datasets – transfers directly.
Recommendation: be transparent with the client that 190 hours is an optimistic estimate and that Deliverable 2 carries the highest technical risk of any Phase 2 deliverable. If the budget is firm, consider scoping Deliverable 2 as “exploratory” rather than “comprehensive” – e.g., focus on the top 3-4 agencies with the most standardized EIS formats rather than trying to cover all 60.

title: Phase 2 Deliverable Assessment
text:
Before diving into each deliverable, the overarching lessons from Phase 1 are critical:

Messy, unstructured data is the constant enemy. Metadata is sparse, text formats are inconsistent across agencies, and even “simple” extraction tasks (like finding a decision date with a signature block) required multi-iteration pipeline development (regex -> hybrid LLM -> BERT -> 11+ refinements).
Initiation-style tasks (finding implicit information) are far harder than decision-style tasks (finding explicit information). BERT decision coverage hit 85%, but initiation stalled at 16% – and that gap persists despite extensive pattern expansion and class rebalancing. Phase 2 deliverables lean heavily toward the “initiation” end of this spectrum (implicit, contextual, requires reasoning).
Local LLMs (Llama 3.2 3B) work for classification but struggle with comprehension. The hybrid timeline approach showed this clearly: the LLM can label “is this a decision date?” but it can’t reliably reason about why a project triggered NEPA or what constitutes significant impact.
Every extraction task took 2-3x the initially estimated time once you factor in validation, false positive triage, class imbalance, and re-runs.

title: Phase 2 Deliverable Assessment
text:
Difficulty: MODERATE-HIGH
What it requires: For each project, identify why NEPA was triggered – federal land, federal funding, federal permits, or some combination. This means reading project documents and classifying the federal nexus.
What works in your favor: - The lead agency is already in the metadata and is often a strong proxy (BLM -> federal land; DOE -> federal funding). You could get 60-70% coverage from metadata-based heuristics alone before touching document text. - The “trigger” language is sometimes explicit: “This EA is prepared because the proposed action involves a federal lease on BLM-managed land.” - Regex can catch many explicit patterns.
Problems I foresee: - Many documents don’t explicitly state why NEPA was triggered – the federal nexus is assumed by context. A CE for a cell tower on National Forest land doesn’t say “because it’s on federal land”; it just says “Coldfoot Cell Tower, Tongass National Forest.” - Distinguishing “mentioned” from “triggered by” is hard. A project might discuss federal funding in one section but the actual trigger is federal land use. - Multiple triggers per project is common and ambiguous. - 445K targeted pages is large. Even with 30% prefiltering, you’re sending ~134K pages to an LLM. - A local 3B model likely can’t do this well. This is a comprehension/inference task, not just pattern matching.
Realistic time estimate: 35-50 hours
High-level plan:

Build a metadata-based heuristic classifier (agency -> trigger type mapping) – covers the easy cases (~60-70%) (5 hrs)
Develop regex patterns for explicit trigger language (“federal land,” “DOE funding,” “Section 404 permit,” etc.) (5 hrs)
Run regex extraction on the full corpus with prefiltering (3 hrs)
For ambiguous/missing cases, design an LLM prompt and test on a 50-project sample – evaluate whether Llama 3B is sufficient or you need an enterprise model (8 hrs)
Full LLM run on remaining unresolved cases (5 hrs)
Manual validation on a stratified sample of ~50-100 projects (5 hrs)
Iterate on false positives/negatives, re-run (5-10 hrs)
Analysis & visualization (4 hrs)





Difficulty: HIGH – This is the hardest deliverable and the highest risk
What it requires: For FEIS/DEIS documents, extract which resource areas (air quality, water, wildlife, cultural resources, etc.) were found to have “significant impacts.” Then, starting with mitigated FONSIs, identify cases where impacts would have been significant but were mitigated.
What works in your favor: - EIS documents are relatively structured – they typically have chapters organized by resource area (Chapter 3: Affected Environment, Chapter 4: Environmental Consequences). - The vocabulary of significance is somewhat formulaic (“significant adverse impact,” “less than significant with mitigation,” etc.). - Only ~371K pages from FEIS/DEIS documents, which is a smaller subset.
Problems I foresee – and they are serious: - No standard format across agencies. DOI, DOE, USDA, DOD all structure their impact analyses differently. Some use tables, some use narrative, some use a hybrid. Section numbering varies. - Significance language is highly nuanced. “The proposed action would result in significant impacts to…” vs. “The proposed action would not result in significant impacts to…” – these differ by one word. Worse, many documents use hedging: “potentially significant,” “significant but mitigable,” “significant and unavoidable.” - Mitigated FONSIs are exceptionally tricky. You need to identify that (a) an EA found potentially significant impacts, AND (b) mitigation measures reduced them below significance, AND (c) the FONSI was issued with conditions. This is a multi-step reasoning chain. - A 3B local model will almost certainly fail at this task. This requires reading comprehension, not pattern matching. The distinction between “significant” and “not significant” in environmental documents is exactly the kind of nuanced language understanding that requires a large model. - Resource area segmentation adds another dimension – you’re not just classifying significance for the whole document, but for ~10-15 different resource areas per document.
Realistic time estimate: 55-75 hours
This is where I’d most strongly recommend budgeting for enterprise LLMs (GPT-4o, Claude Sonnet). The $115 estimate in the proposal assumes cost-efficient mini models with 30% prefiltering – but the accuracy of a mini model on this task will likely be poor, and you may need the full-capability model. At GPT-4o pricing, 371K pages could run $300-500+ depending on context length.
High-level plan:

Define the taxonomy of resource areas and significance levels (with client input) (3 hrs)
Identify the structural patterns of EIS chapters across the top 5-6 agencies – map how they organize resource area analysis (6 hrs)
Build a document structure parser that identifies relevant sections/chapters (avoiding appendices, references, etc.) (8 hrs)
Design the LLM extraction prompt – test on 20 FEIS documents with both a local model and an enterprise model, compare accuracy (8 hrs)
Decision point: If local model accuracy is <70%, switch to enterprise LLM (likely outcome)
Full extraction run with enterprise LLM, focusing on identified relevant sections (6 hrs)
Mitigated FONSI sub-pipeline: identify FONSIs with mitigation conditions, extract the resource areas and mitigation types (10 hrs additional – this is essentially a second extraction task)
Validation on a stratified sample (5 hrs)
Analysis & visualization (5 hrs)





Difficulty: MODERATE
What it requires: Compare fossil fuel vs. clean energy and linear vs. non-linear project reviews across CE/EA/EIS rates, timelines, geography, and other dimensions.
What works in your favor: - This is primarily an analytical/comparative deliverable, not an extraction one. Most of the underlying data already exists from Phase 1. - The energy type classification is already built (clean/fossil/other). - Linear vs. non-linear can be derived from existing project type tags (transmission, pipelines = linear; generation = non-linear). - The 788K page count in the proposal seems high – this may be for validation or supplementary extraction, but the core analysis uses already-extracted data.
Problems I foresee: - Depends heavily on timeline quality. If initiation coverage remains at 16%, the timeline comparisons between fossil fuel and clean energy will be based on incomplete data. Duration statistics could be misleading. - Sample sizes for some categories may be small. Fossil fuel EIS projects vs. clean energy EIS projects – are there enough of each for meaningful comparison? - The “visual impacts” mention in the proposal is vague and could turn into a significant extraction task if it means actually identifying visual impact discussions in documents.
Realistic time estimate: 30-40 hours
High-level plan:

Create the linear/non-linear classification from existing project types (3 hrs)
Merge all Phase 1 + Phase 2 extracted datasets (timelines, capacity, reviews, geography) (4 hrs)
Build comparison tables: CE/EA/EIS rates by fossil vs. clean, linear vs. non-linear (5 hrs)
Timeline comparison analysis (duration by energy type, project type) – depends on D4 timeline quality (6 hrs)
Geographic analysis: where do fossil vs. clean energy reviews happen? (4 hrs)
Statistical testing and visualization (6 hrs)
Write-up and narrative (5 hrs)





Difficulty: MODERATE-HIGH
What it requires: Extend the Phase 1 BERT timeline pipeline to categorical exclusions (CEs), cross-reference Federal Register NOIs, and perform segmentation/outlier analysis.
What works in your favor: - The BERT pipeline infrastructure is built and battle-tested. - Decision coverage is decent at 85%. - Federal Register linking code already exists (code/extract/federal_register.py, data/analysis/noi_federal_register.parquet). - The segmentation analysis (pre/post-FRA, by agency, by year) is straightforward once timelines exist.
Problems I foresee: - CE documents are fundamentally different from EA/EIS documents. They’re often 1-3 page forms, sometimes with checkbox dates, sometimes with no narrative at all. The current regex/BERT approach was tuned for EA/EIS-style documents with signature blocks and narrative text. CE forms may need a different extraction approach entirely. - Initiation remains the Achilles’ heel. At 16% coverage, you can’t compute meaningful durations for most projects. The Phase 1 experience suggests this won’t improve dramatically without manual labeling or fundamentally different data sources (like Federal Register NOIs). - Federal Register NOI matching is fuzzy. Matching a NEPATEC project to its corresponding Federal Register NOI requires name/agency/date matching, which is error-prone. - CE projects are the vast majority (~20K of ~22K clean energy projects) but many may have trivially short timelines, skewing any aggregate analysis.
Realistic time estimate: 30-45 hours
High-level plan:

Analyze a sample of 50 CE documents to understand their structure and date patterns – determine if BERT approach transfers or needs adaptation (5 hrs)
If CE forms need new patterns: expand regex patterns, regenerate training data, retrain BERT (8 hrs)
Run BERT on full CE corpus (1-2 hrs compute time)
Federal Register NOI cross-referencing: improve fuzzy matching, validate on sample (6 hrs)
Use NOI dates as initiation fallback where BERT initiation is missing (3 hrs)
Segmentation analysis: pre/post-FRA, by agency, by project type, by year (5 hrs)
Outlier identification and case study selection (4 hrs)
Visualization (3 hrs)





Difficulty: MODERATE (but open-ended)
What it requires: Cluster FONSI documents by project type and mitigation measures to identify patterns that could support new categorical exclusion (CE) development.
What works in your favor: - Only 5,760 pages – orders of magnitude smaller than other deliverables. - FONSIs are relatively short, structured documents. - Modern embedding models (even local ones) can produce good document representations for clustering. - The client has a clear use case (supporting regulatory CE development), which gives the analysis a target.
Problems I foresee: - “Patterns” is vague. What constitutes a useful pattern for CE development? This needs careful scoping with the client. Are you looking for: project types that routinely get FONSIs (suggesting they could be CEs)? Common mitigation conditions? Resource areas that consistently come up? - Mitigation measure extraction is itself an NLP task. Mitigation conditions vary from “The project shall install erosion control barriers” to “The applicant agrees to the following 47 conditions…” – extracting and categorizing these could be a full pipeline. - Clustering can produce garbage. If the document features aren’t well-chosen, you’ll get clusters that don’t mean anything actionable.
Realistic time estimate: 18-30 hours (depends on how deep the client wants to go)
High-level plan:

Scope with client: define what “patterns” means for CE development – what would an actionable finding look like? (2 hrs)
Extract FONSI document text, filter to main document body (3 hrs)
Generate document embeddings (can start with local sentence-transformers model) (2 hrs)
Cluster analysis: try topic modeling (LDA) and embedding-based clustering (k-means on embeddings) (4 hrs)
Identify cluster themes and validate with domain knowledge (3 hrs)
If mitigation extraction is in scope: regex + LLM pipeline for mitigation conditions (6 hrs)
Synthesize findings into actionable recommendations (3 hrs)





Difficulty: MODERATE (time-consuming but well-scoped)

title: EA Page Viewer
text:
Simple notebook to view EA document pages for manual review and exploration.
import re
import pandas as pd
from pathlib import Path

# Display settings
pd.set_option('display.max_colwidth', None)
pd.set_option('display.max_rows', 100)

title: EA Page Viewer
text:
Load Data

# Load CE documents
documents = pd.read_parquet('../data/analysis/documents_combined.parquet')
ea_documents = documents[documents["dataset_source"] == "EA"]
print(f"Loaded {len(ea_documents):,} EA documents")

def page_num_int(value):
    """Extract first numeric token from page labels like '1', 'Page-1', or '1-6'."""
    if pd.isna(value):
        return pd.NA
    match = re.search(r"(\d+)", str(value))
    if match:
        return int(match.group(1))
    return pd.NA

# Load CE pages
ea_pages = pd.read_parquet('../data/processed/ea/pages.parquet')
ea_pages["_page_number_num"] = ea_pages["page_number"].map(page_num_int).astype("Int64")
print(f"Loaded {len(ea_pages):,} EA pages")

Loaded 14,242 EA documents
Loaded 469,106 EA pages

title: EA Page Viewer
text:
Helper Functions

def list_documents(project_id):
    """List all documents for a given project."""
    docs = ea_documents[ea_documents["project_id"] == project_id]
    if len(docs) == 0:
        print(f"No documents found for project_id: {project_id}")
        return None
    
    print(f"\nDocuments for project: {project_id}")
    print("-" * 80)
    display_cols = ["document_id", "document_type", "document_type_category", 
                    "main_document", "file_name", "total_pages"]
    available_cols = [c for c in display_cols if c in docs.columns]
    return docs[available_cols]


def view_page(document_id, page_num=1):
    """View a specific page from a document."""
    page_target = page_num_int(page_num)
    if pd.isna(page_target):
        print(f"Invalid page number: {page_num}")
        return None

    page = ea_pages[(ea_pages["document_id"] == document_id) & 
                    (ea_pages["_page_number_num"] == page_target)]
    
    if len(page) == 0:
        print(f"Page {page_num} not found for document_id: {document_id}")
        return None
    
    # Get document metadata
    doc = ea_documents[ea_documents["document_id"] == document_id]
    if len(doc) > 0:
        print(f"\n{'='*80}")
        print(f"Document: {doc.iloc[0].get('file_name', 'N/A')}")
        print(f"Type: {doc.iloc[0].get('document_type', 'N/A')} | "
              f"Category: {doc.iloc[0].get('document_type_category', 'N/A')} | "
              f"Main: {doc.iloc[0].get('main_document', 'N/A')}")
        print(f"{'='*80}")
    
    print(f"\n--- PAGE {page_num} ---\n")
    print(page.iloc[0]["page_text"])
    print(f"\n--- END PAGE {page_num} ---\n")
    return page.iloc[0]["page_text"]


def view_pages(document_id, start_page=1, end_page=5):
    """View a range of pages from a document."""
    # Get document metadata
    doc = ea_documents[ea_documents["document_id"] == document_id]
    if len(doc) > 0:
        print(f"\n{'='*80}")
        print(f"Document: {doc.iloc[0].get('file_name', 'N/A')}")
        print(f"Type: {doc.iloc[0].get('document_type', 'N/A')} | "
              f"Category: {doc.iloc[0].get('document_type_category', 'N/A')} | "
              f"Main: {doc.iloc[0].get('main_document', 'N/A')}")
        print(f"{'='*80}")
    
    for page_num in range(start_page, end_page + 1):
        page = ea_pages[(ea_pages["document_id"] == document_id) & 
                        (ea_pages["_page_number_num"] == page_num)]
        if len(page) > 0:
            print(f"\n--- PAGE {page_num} ---\n")
            print(page.iloc[0]["page_text"])
            print(f"\n--- END PAGE {page_num} ---\n")
        else:
            print(f"Page {page_num} not found")
            break


def view_project_pages(project_id, document_id=None):
    """View all pages of each document in a project (no truncation).
    
    Args:
        project_id: The project ID to filter documents
        document_id: Optional document ID to view only that specific document
    """
    docs = ea_documents[ea_documents["project_id"] == project_id]
    
    # Filter by document_id if provided
    if document_id is not None:
        docs = docs[docs["document_id"] == document_id]
        
    if len(docs) == 0:
        if document_id is not None:
            print(f"No document found with document_id: {document_id} in project_id: {project_id}")
        else:
            print(f"No documents found for project_id: {project_id}")
        return
        
    for _, doc in docs.iterrows():
        doc_id = doc["document_id"]
        print(f"\n{'='*80}")
        print(f"Document: {doc.get('file_name', 'N/A')}")
        print(
            f"Type: {doc.get('document_type', 'N/A')} | "
            f"Category: {doc.get('document_type_category', 'N/A')} | "
            f"Main: {doc.get('main_document', 'N/A')}"
        )
        print(f"{'='*80}")
                
        doc_pages = (
            ea_pages[ea_pages["document_id"] == doc_id]
            .sort_values(["_page_number_num", "page_number"], na_position="last")
        )
                
        for _, page in doc_pages.iterrows():
            print(f"\n--- PAGE {page['page_number']} ---\n")
            print(page["page_text"])


def search_pages(project_id, search_term):
    """Search for a term in all pages of a project."""
    docs = ea_documents[ea_documents["project_id"] == project_id]
    doc_ids = docs["document_id"].tolist()
    
    matching_pages = ea_pages[
        (ea_pages["document_id"].isin(doc_ids)) & 
        (ea_pages["page_text"].str.contains(search_term, case=False, na=False))
    ]
    
    print(f"\nFound {len(matching_pages)} pages containing '{search_term}'")
    print("-" * 80)
    
    for _, page in matching_pages.iterrows():
        doc = docs[docs["document_id"] == page["document_id"]].iloc[0]
        print(f"\nDocument: {doc.get('file_name', 'N/A')} | Page: {page['page_number']}")
        
        # Show context around the search term
        text = page["page_text"]
        idx = text.lower().find(search_term.lower())
        if idx >= 0:
            start = max(0, idx - 200)
            end = min(len(text), idx + len(search_term) + 200)
            context = text[start:end]
            if start > 0:
                context = "..." + context
            if end < len(text):
                context = context + "..."
            print(context)
    
    return matching_pages


def get_random_project(n_docs=2):
    """Get a random project with at least n_docs documents."""
    import random
    doc_counts = ea_documents.groupby("project_id").size()
    eligible = doc_counts[doc_counts >= n_docs].index.tolist()
    
    project_id = random.choice(eligible)
    print(f"Random project with {doc_counts[project_id]} documents: {project_id}")
    return project_id

“Planned actions in response to wildfires, floods, weather events, earthquakes, or

management-approved condition as a result of the event. Such activities shall be limited

text:
Programmatic & Tiered Reviews


There are three types of reviews in the NEPA process:

Standard: Stand-alone EA or EIS covering a single project — the default NEPA approach
Programmatic (Tier 1): Broad “umbrella” review (PEIS/PEA) covering a class of actions or a region, usually before site-specific work begins
Tiered (Tier 2): Site-specific review that builds on a prior programmatic review, scopes out specific issues already identified, streamline the review process
















Standard review is the overwhelming norm — Almost 90% of projects use the standalone standard review process.
Tiered reviews are more rare

The Nuclear Regulatory Commission and BLM drive Other Independent Agencies and Department of Interior non-standard review use – check out our analysis on the website

title: NEPA Decarbonization Technologies Analysis
text:
Are Tiered Reviews Actually Faster?
















Tiered EAs take longer than standard EAs on average — but they are substantially shorter than a full EIS, suggesting the real efficiency gain from tiering is when it allows an agency to avoid a full EIS altogether rather than just shortening an EA.
Tiered EISs take less time than standard and programmatic EISs, though distributions substantially overlap and sample sizes are small.
WORD OF CAUTION: Small sample for non-standard reviews is still quite small to draw strong conclusions here.

section: How Long Does NEPA Review Take?
text:
How Long Does NEPA Review Take?














Timeline completeness (projects with both initiation + decision dates):





The CE→EA→EIS duration gradient is steep: median durations range from ~1 month (CE) to ~14 months (EA) to ~34 months (EIS) — a rather large difference.
The long tail drives NEPA’s reputation: 10% of EIS reviews exceed 7.5 years, but this is not typical — the median is 3 years.
Timeline completeness is partial: only 30% of CEs have extractable dates; EA (62%) and EIS (48%) are better but not complete, so medians likely undercount the slowest cases.

title: NEPA Decarbonization Technologies Analysis
text:
Phase 1 Summary: Key Findings


D1: DOE Categorical Exclusions are king: DOE handles 81% of review cases, processing 96% via CE
D1: Western states and federal lands dominate — BLM, Forest Service, and DOE public land concentration drives the geographic pattern
D2: Tiering might help — tiered EAs take longer than standard EAs — but less time than a full EIS
D3: Duration gradient is steep with a long tail — CE (~1 mo) → EA (~14 mo) → EIS (~3 yr median)
D3: Policy stimulus — ARRA (2010) and IRA/BIL (2022–23), CE peaks are clear
D3: Scale matches review intensity — EIS = median 538 MW; EA = 60 MW; CE = 1.2 MW
D4: DOE is the multi-agency hub — improving DOE-DOI-USDA coordination would have outsized impact
D5: FRA had effect but not definitive — document lengths declined; most projects are compliant (small N)
D6: No relation between line length and duration, but long lines (100+ miles) take longer (small N)

title: NEPA Decarbonization Technologies Analysis
text:
D3-Timeline Extraction Methodology


Two-Stage BERT Pipeline

Date extraction — identify all dates in document text with surrounding sentence context (±2 sentences)
Classification — fine-tuned BERT model assigns each date to:

Initiation — NOI, application received, scoping notice
Review — draft publication, comment period
Decision — ROD, FONSI, approval signature
Other — expiration dates, referenced past actions


Selection rules:

Decision: prioritize strong signature/approval cues
Initiation: NOI > application > scoping (in priority order)
Fallback: use earliest review date when no initiation found


Coverage Limitations






Warning



CE (30%): Short documents have less temporal information
EIS (48%): RODs often issued as separate documents not linked in dataset
EA (62%): Best coverage; FONSIs typically included in the same document




Model: BERT (bert-base-uncased), fine-tuned on manually annotated NEPA document sentences. Class imbalance for initiation dates is a known limitation.

D5-FRA Regulatory vs. Raw Pages Methodology


Regulatory Page Calculation

Extract body text from OCR’d PDF
Detect appendix boundaries using section-header patterns (e.g., “Appendix A”, “References”, “List of Preparers”)
Count words in body text (pre-appendix sections only)
Regulatory pages = body word count ÷ 500

Scale of difference:

EAs: regulatory pages ≈ 45–55% of raw page count
EISs: regulatory pages ≈ 70–80% of raw page count


Known Edge Cases






Warning



OCR errors in scanned legacy documents may produce NULL word counts
Non-standard appendix headers may not be detected
~5% of cases: regulatory pages exceed raw pages (OCR text extraction artifact in table-heavy documents)
Waivers and “extraordinary complexity” exceptions are not distinguished from standard non-compliance
